Thursday's PM close was a risk-off shock centered on tech. The S&P 500 fell 4.36% to 7353.73 (from 7688.62 the prior session) and the Nasdaq Composite fell 5.52% to 24315.0. The Dow lost 3.44% and the Russell 2000 lost 4.45%. The VIX jumped 69.66% to 28.18 from 16.61. US Info Tech fell 7.3% on the day and is down 16.87% over a month. Investors bought havens. The US 2Y fell 11.86bp to 4.4623% and the 10Y fell 5.32bp to 4.8347%, a bull steepener that suggests the market is pricing more Fed help. Brent rose 5.16% to 99.5 and WTI rose 2.72% to 90.52; no verified news source tied this to Iran today. Gold was flat at 4088.21 and the dollar did not move (DXY 101.586). The tech-analog phase model still classifies the drawdown as Phase 1 (initial drop, credit calm), 22 days after the peak, with a tech-basket drawdown of -0.2367. Three signposts have now triggered: Nasdaq volatility (VXN 38.26 vs the 35 trigger), breadth (0.7857 of basket names more than 20% off their highs vs 0.5) and semis (SOX -0.3843 from its 52-week high vs -0.3). The VIX is 1.82 from its 30 gauge. The phase model puts the odds of reaching Phase 2 or worse within 12 months at 0.734, up 18.0pp versus the prior session. Its 6-month Phase 3 odds are 0.112 and its 6-month Phase 4 odds are 0.218. These are model estimates, not certainties. HY contagion: the stress in the lowest-rated junk bonds is real and climbing. The Caa-B gap is 782bp, at the 99.53rd percentile of its 5-year range (avg5y ~418bp), up 80bp in a month and 222bp in 3 months, and the widest since 2020-04-16. Single-B spreads widened 26bp in a month to 310bp, and the 63-day Caa/B correlation rose to 0.709 from 0.353 three months ago, now above its 5-year median of 0.693. That pattern fits CCC stress starting to bleed into single-B. BB (195bp, d1m 18bp) and IG (89bp) remain near their 5-year medians, so it has not reached the top of the quality ladder. This is descriptive, not a validated signal. AI backstop: CoreWeave 5Y CDS is 1184.58bp, 9.92bp below its 1,194.5bp Oct 15 record, at 98.66% of its run from the June low. It widened 38.59bp on the day. Nvidia CDS tightened 5.97bp to 138.96bp, so the market is still separating the guarantor from the neoclouds even as CoreWeave equity is down 64.91% from its high. Sentiment is fearful but not panicked. Bloomberg's credit OAS prints (IG 0.89%, HY 3.24%) look like they carry the prior close and do not yet reflect today's equity break.

“Tech blinked and the VIX nearly doubled, but until the CCC rot climbs the junk ladder into BB and IG, this is still a Phase 1 equity scare, not a credit event.”
📊Markets

Losses were broad but led by growth. The Nasdaq Comp fell 5.52% (-1421.51 to 24315.0), the S&P 500 fell 4.36% (-334.89 to 7353.73), the Russell 2000 fell 4.45% (to 2729.887) and the Dow fell 3.44% (to 51523.06). Overseas markets fell far less: the Euro Stoxx 50 lost 0.55%, the STOXX 600 lost 0.38%, the FTSE 100 lost 0.43% and the Nikkei 225 lost 1.79%. Most of their sessions closed before the US selloff deepened. The VIX closed at 28.18 (+69.66%). Rates rallied: the 2Y fell to 4.4623% (-11.86bp), the 10Y to 4.8347% (-5.32bp) and the 30Y to 5.2539% (-2.23bp). The Bund (3.241%) and JGB 10Y (2.785%) also fell. The Gilt 10Y was the outlier, edging up to 5.132%. In commodities, Brent rose 5.16% to 99.5 and WTI rose 2.72% to 90.52, while copper fell 2.47% to 627.0, a growth-scare signal. Gold (4088.21) and silver (51.7787) were flat.

Two-sided analog episodes per signal: days where the signal's percentile-rank (vs its own full history) was <=5th or >=95th, or |z-score|>=1.3, clustered into one episode per zone per >=6-month gap between episode starts. For each zone, the realized forward 6-month % change in the BENCHMARK'S OUTRIGHT PRICE from each episode start is measured; a card's direction (BUY/SELL) is whichever sign that median historical move carries. Entry/target/stretch/stop are computed directly from this table -- the narrative prose (thesis/rationale) is the only part supplied by an LLM, and it is not permitted to alter a number. Crack spreads and curve shapes are, financially, relative-value signals rather than clean predictors of outright price; expressing every card in outright price terms is a deliberate simplification. HO36 Comdty (ULSD's 36-month point) is thin/less liquid on this seat -- treat its curve-shape reading with lower confidence than the others. Not investment advice.

Churn = the longest window of 20-120 sessions whose close range is <= 8x its median ATR(14), with median ADX(14) < 20, an insignificant close-price slope (p > 0.05), and >= 2 entries into each edge zone (top/bottom 20% of the band). Support/resistance = median swing low/high (+/-5 sessions); outer edges = the window's extreme closes. Breakout = a close beyond the outer edge by > 0.5 ATR, confirmed by a second close or one close beyond 1 ATR. A break back inside within 5 sessions is a failed break. An episode's outer edges can widen at most 0.5 ATR past their first detection, so a slow grind can't drag the range along with it. Base rates come from replaying the same rules over the full history, day by day, with no lookahead. This is pattern analysis of historical prices, not investment advice.

💧Treasury liquidity & rates volcomputed

US Govt Securities Liquidity Index (GVLQUSD), MOVE, Fed DKW term premium and TLT option skew, live from Bloomberg + federalreserve.gov.

Five charts tracking the mechanism Simon White laid out for why Treasury liquidity is deteriorating: rising inflation volatility feeds into a higher term premium, which steepens the curve, which raises bond vol, which shows up as worse UST market liquidity. Right now UST liquidity is at the 50th percentile of its own history (higher = worse) and the Fed's own DKW real term premium is +91bp.

Latest reading is +0.38 vol points (5th percentile of the 61 runs recorded so far). Positive means the 5%-OTM put is pricier than the at-the-money option -- the market paying up for downside-price / higher-yield insurance on long-end Treasuries.

UST liquidity index is 1.53 (50th percentile of its own 2007-present history -- 100th = worst liquidity on record), improving over the past 3 months (-0.08 pts). CPI YoY volatility (2yr) is 0.50pp; the article's thesis is that rising inflation vol drags liquidity worse, which this chart is built to let you check month to month.

Real term premium is +91bp (96th percentile of its own 2007-present history), up 12bp over the trailing ~2 months. Inflation risk premium is +14bp. Fed staff's own DKW decomposition (D'Amico-Kim-Wei, updated Kim-Walsh-Wei) splits the rise in long yields into a policy-uncertainty component (real term premium) and an inflation-uncertainty component -- both rising is the article's read that this move isn't just a rate-expectations story.

MOVE is 97.9 (70th percentile of its own post-2007 history). The 3m10s curve is 74bp (flatter by 10bp over 3 months). The article's claim is mechanical, not just correlated -- a steeper curve gives forward rates more room to move before converging to spot, which is itself higher realized/implied vol.

MOVE and the UST liquidity index have moved together with a full-history correlation of +0.72 (both series read as 'worse' when they rise). That's the closing link in the article's chain: inflation vol -> term premium -> curve steepness -> bond vol -> liquidity.

Term premium is the Fed's own DKW model series (D'Amico-Kim-Wei, updated Kim-Walsh-Wei), pulled directly from federalreserve.gov, not Bloomberg. Not a trading signal -- a liquidity/vol monitor only.

Same test on each trailing window: cup base = lowest close in the window, left rim = highest close before it, right rim = highest close after it. Cup complete at ≥90% retracement; above 110% the yield has run past the old high (a breakout, not a cup). No cup inside the window when its left rim is not the highest close of the 91 days before it, i.e. yields were already falling into the window. Pass level = cup base + 0.90 × (left rim − cup base).

🗞️Street View — Where the Cycle Is HeadingCURATED · AS OF 2026-10-01

⚠ Commentary is 35 days old (as of 2026-10-01); it may not reflect the latest Fed news.

Consensus is a short, shallow campaign: one or two more 25bp hikes, December more likely than October. The debate is whether hiking into an energy shock ends in recession, and the bond market is already doing some of the tightening.

The Fed

  • Sept 16: unanimous 25bp hike to 3.75–4.00%, the first since 2023. Dots: median one more hike in 2026; 16 of 18 see at least one, 4 see two. Inflation not back at 2% until 2029. (CNBC, FedAndMarkets)
  • Warsh's message was distinctly hawkish (inflation 'too high and broad-based'); the Conference Board calls it 'not a one and done'. (Conference Board)
  • Sept 29, Williams (NY Fed): 'no need for urgency'; one more hike 'late this year' may be appropriate; the biggest inflation shocks have passed. (Bloomberg, NY Fed)
  • Sept 30, August PCE came in soft: headline 3.4% (vs 3.7% expected), core 3.0% (vs 3.3%). October odds fell; December still priced. Kashkari: inflation 'still too high'. (CNBC, CNBC (Kashkari))

Market pricing

  • October 28 hike odds vary widely by venue, roughly 35% to 69% (prediction markets highest, CME futures ~58%), mostly measured before the soft PCE print. (PredictionMarketsPicks)
  • About 83% odds of another hike by year-end; futures price ~93bp of tightening over the next 9 meetings, more than the dots. (Forbes)

Bonds and credit

  • 10-year Treasury above 5.25% (Sept 28), the highest since 2007; 30-year ~5.49%. Drivers cited: sticky energy inflation (Iran war), heavy issuance, AI capex demand. Term premium ~1.0–1.4%. (CNBC, CNBC (Warsh's yield problem))
  • AI-related issuers trade ~115bp vs ~78bp for IG overall; high-yield AI supply $40B year to date vs $12B in all of 2025. BNP and Goldman warn the issuance could pressure spreads. (Reuters, Bloomberg (BNP))

The bear case

  • Rosenberg: the Fed has never hiked into an energy shock without a recession, and AI won't save it this time. (TheStreet)
  • Goldman called the case for hiking 'weak' (demand not overheating, energy inflation should fade when the war ends). Oxford Economics: 'The Fed cannot control energy prices'; the risk is a weaker labor market. (CNN)

Read-through: For bonds, the bigger risk is the long end, not the Fed: term premium and supply keeping the 10-year above 5% matter more than one extra 25bp. The recession call is loud but isn't in any sell-side house view yet.

Curated summary of published Fed, market and economist commentary (news and research via the web), not a computed series and not a forecast. Odds differ by venue and move daily.

🔥Is Inflation Persistent?

Persistence score: 58/100 — Inflation is sticky but not re-accelerating at the core. Core PCE is 3.12% YoY and Core CPI 2.6%. The underlying measures cluster at 2.26-2.82%: median CPI 2.61% (falling), trimmed-mean CPI 2.66% (flat), median PCE 2.67% (flat), sticky CPI 2.82% and core sticky 2.78% (flat). All sit roughly mid-to-upper range versus history per the computed core-trend panel. The pressure is coming from the volatile end: flexible CPI is 6.12% and rising. Breadth is two-sided. The Dallas Fed distribution shows 16.6% of the PCE basket rising above 10% and another 10.2% at 5-10%, but 25.6% of items are falling. Wages are not driving it (AHE 3.0%, ECI 0.8%), and breakevens are anchored (1y 2.0263%, 5y 2.273%). With Brent at 99.5, the risk is that energy feeds the flexible component further. Analyst read: a persistent, energy-tilted inflation problem rather than a wage-price spiral.

🫧Tech Bubble Peak Again?vs March 2000
BUBBLE RESEMBLANCE · SUPER COUNT computed
7 of 22 indicators at peak-like levels · 6 beyond 2000 — 55/100
Today does not look like March 2000 on equity froth. The computed indicators show the Nasdaq trailing P/E at 38.31x vs 175x (15% of the way to peak conditions), the Nasdaq 3.1% below its 200DMA (0%) and SOX P/E at 31.89x (30%). The late-cycle catalyst and macro-regime panels are a different story. IG spread tightness (126%), Baa-10Y tightness (145%), loose financial conditions per the NFCI (148%) and cheap commodities vs equities (200%) are at or beyond 2000-peak conditions; the 2s10s curve is at 65%. Signposts are mixed: put/call complacency is at 88%, while VIX complacency (26%) and AAII bullishness (14%) have already flipped to fear. The phase model places the tech basket in Phase 1 (initial drop, credit calm), with 1-month odds of P1 0.565 and P2 0.4. It puts the odds of reaching Phase 2 or worse within 12 months at 0.734 and within 24 months at 0.816, with 24-month Phase 4 (trough/recovery) odds of 0.746. These are model estimates.

Bubble-analog — today's Nasdaq vs the dot-com cycle (two anchors)

WHY TWO START DATES?
Each line is rebased to 100 at a low the tech bull launched from, so elapsed time lines up. Oct-2022 is today's anchor — it was the prior bear-market bottom. Oct-1990 is the dot-com cycle's equivalent (its literal prior bear bottom). But 1990 predates the internet mania by ~4 years, so the second chart re-anchors the dot-com line to the 1994 reset low, just before the surge ignited, for a tighter like-for-like. Today sits very early under the strict 1990 analog, further along under the 1994 surge analog.
━ Anchored at the prior bear-market bottom (Oct-1990)   ━ today's cycle
━ Anchored at the pre-internet reset low (1994)   ━ today's cycle

Valuation marker: today's Nasdaq P/E (38x) ≈ 22% of the ~175x 2000-peak P/E.

IF THIS RHYMES WITH 2000
Nasdaq fell -78.0% peak→trough (2000-03-10 → 2002-10-09, ~31 months); it took ~15 years to reclaim the high.

The 2000 analog is no longer about valuation mania. It is about the sequence. In 2000 the tech bust started with an equity drop while credit stayed calm, then credit cracked (Phase 2), then the economy and banks (Phase 3). Today matches Phase 1: the tech basket is down 23.67% (vs -15.69% for the 2000 basket on the same day count), and three signposts (VXN, breadth, SOX) have triggered. Meanwhile, the HMM regime model reads 0.998 'Calm (Phase-1-like)' and credit regime 0.971 'Credit calm'. The bridge to Phase 2 runs through credit: HY OAS 324bp vs triggers at 420bp/448bp, and Baa-10Y 158.53bp vs 195.07bp. The early warning is already visible in CCC spreads and CoreWeave CDS. The fundamental cushion is -0.047. Economy signposts are far from their triggers (Sahm 0.0 vs 0.5; ISM 54.5 vs 47). The model's historical tilt at this phase mix favours gold, Treasury duration and IG credit over mega-cap growth, developed international and EM. The five tech-bubble inputs (concentration 38%, IPO froth 40, CAPE 35x, Buffett ratio 195%, long-term EPS growth 65) are rough analyst estimates. They were not verified by web search this run, and none of today's searches returned a source for them.

Positioning tilt (generic, historical): Historically, at this phase mix the phase-conditional optimum has favoured gold, Treasury duration and investment-grade credit, over mega-cap growth, developed international and emerging markets.

Phases are rules with the same thresholds in 2000 and today: Phase 2 = HY OAS +150bp or Baa-10y +50bp from the basket's peak; Phase 3 = Sahm rule or ISM < 47 for 3 months AND bank stress (KBW -25% or C&I charge-offs >= 1% and rising); Phase 4 = basket +20% off its low, above its 200-day average, HY 150bp off its wide. Odds come from every Nasdaq-100 drop since 1985 that reached today's depth, weighted by how closely its credit, macro and volatility readings matched today's, plus a small labelled judgment overlay for AI-credit stress. 'Ever P2+' = chance spreads cross the Phase-2 line at any point before the horizon. Model estimates on ~40 episodes: read them to within +/-10 points. Not financial advice.

🏦Fed Chair Warsh
NEAR TERM

Inference: a hold at the next meeting. Under Warsh the Fed held at 3.50-3.75% at his June 17 debut with a hawkish, inflation-first tone, and the outcome of the Oct 27-28 meeting could not be verified. Today's 11.86bp drop in the 2Y shows the market leaning toward easing after the equity shock. With core PCE at 3.12% and Brent near 99.5, a Warsh Fed is more likely to talk through the selloff than cut immediately.

~1 YEAR

Inference: June projections showed 9 of 19 policymakers expecting a hike by end-2026, which Warsh did not endorse; he skipped the dot submission. That, plus his 'sweeping review', suggests his first year is more about changing the framework and communication than fast cuts. The chance of a pivot toward cuts rises only if the tech drawdown spreads into credit (Phase 2+) or the labor data weakens. Payrolls are 29k and unemployment 4.2%, so a soft-labor case is building.

Warsh was sworn in as the 17th Fed chair on May 22, 2026. His first FOMC (June 17) held rates unanimously at 3.50-3.75%, which analysts read as hawkish ('inflation remains the priority'). New projections showed 9 of 19 participants anticipating a 2026 hike while Warsh declined to submit a dot. He also launched a sweeping review of the Fed's operations. The October CPI release is scheduled for Nov 10. The near-term and one-year calls above are inferences from these on-record actions, not from any statement made this week. No recent Warsh speech was found in this search.
